headline: Australian investors are willing to pay a premium for right exposures — including beta strategies — in contrast to UK and European investors, but demand for thematics like EM, multi-factor, climate and AI still exceeds adoption
reasoning: Unlike the US and Europe, Australian investors show greater willingness to pay up for access to specific exposures, even beta strategies. However, a gap is forming between investor interest in thematics such as emerging markets, multi-factor, climate, and AI, and actual adoption of those exposures. Currency exposure is also a key consideration for cross-border investing. The gap signals to MSCI where future index product development should focus.
quote: We also see in the Australian market, which differs from the US and Europe, that Australian investors are willing to pay a premium for the right exposures. They're willing to pay a premium for even kind of beta strategies compared to a much lower percentage of people in the UK and Europe... What we're actually seeing in the survey is a gap, a gap is forming between what investors are looking for in terms of the thematics like emerging markets, multi factor strategies, thematics around climate, AI, etcetera. And then the adoption of that is still relatively muted.
episode_title: Why Australian advisers are increasingly looking offshore

headline: Unlike global markets where ETFs are cannibalising managed funds, in Australia both are growing — 73% of advisers plan to increase active ETF allocation, 55% managed funds, and 61% passive ETFs
reasoning: MSCI's global survey shows ETF growth coming at the expense of managed funds internationally, but Australia is a coexistence story where all strategies grow in tandem. At the product level some substitution occurs when a manager launches an ETF version of an existing managed fund strategy, but at the market level it is not a zero-sum game. Fees are the top cited reason for ETF selection, yet 95% of Australian investors already use active ETFs and adoption is set to rise further.
quote: Both are growing. So about 73% of surveyed advisors are looking to increase their allocation to active ETFs, but 55 are also looking to increase their allocation to manage funds. And in the middle, 61% are looking to increase passive ETF adoption as well. So what we're seeing is it's kind of coexistence broadly at the at the market level and all of these strategies are growing together in tandem rather than necessarily cannibalising.

headline: Growing global and Australian focus on emerging markets exposure, alongside demand for AI-related thematics accessible only offshore
reasoning: The desire to look offshore was not unique to Australian respondents — the global survey also showed a strong desire to invest internationally. Emerging markets are attracting increasing attention from all investor types. For Australian investors specifically, lack of domestic AI exposure is an additional driver pushing them to seek international thematics.
quote: I think that trend is here to stay. And it wasn't just the Australia market where we saw that coming through in the in the survey answers, it was also the global survey as well. There's a big desire to look offshore and increasingly there's a focus from all investors on EM on emerging markets... exposure to particular thematics.

headline: 67% of Australian advisers plan to increase international equity allocation over the next two years, driven by concentration risk in domestic banks and mining
reasoning: MSCI survey data shows the majority of Australian advisers want to grow offshore exposure primarily because the Australian market is seen as narrow and concentrated — essentially banks and mining. Advisers are seeking diversification that the domestic market cannot provide. The trend is seen as structural and here to stay, not a short-term reaction to underperformance.
quote: The desire to go internationally is very clear in the survey. The majority of investors are looking to increase their allocation offshore and that is primarily because of concentration actually. So it's a lot of the advisors that responded to the survey put the Australian market in terms of being quite narrow, quite concentrated. It's, you know, essentially banks and mining companies, right. So there's a desire to chase that diversification offshore.
